scores.why: A directly addresses duplicate detection, engineer-approved revision decisions, mandatory metadata and reconciled migration waves, although its effort basis needs validation at this scale; B and C offer credible generic imports but omit those central controls, with B identifying a sign-off owner and C adding metadata design; D supplies basic DAM setup and importing but lacks inventory approval and reconciliation while introducing Content Hub without explaining its entitlement.

A and B describe building and testing reusable templates without migrating preferences or proving suppression, C adds instance setup and CRM mapping but leaves the same essential gaps, and D provides programme inventory, conservative conflict rules, unmatched suppression loading and a first-send gate but insufficient detail on the zero-overlap proof and preservation of settled preferences through sync.

A and D offer data hygiene and scoring with deliverables but do not explain reliable enquiry routing, B is still less complete and concentrates on setup and sync, while C connects form capture, matching and Salesforce ownership with a fallback review but leaves repeated submissions, territory changes and the mechanics of transfer acknowledgement and recovery inadequately specified.

B supplies shared event definitions, restricted payload fields, market-level test outputs and a schedule but leaves collection mechanics, deduplication and consistency verification underdeveloped and its sensitive-field enforcement claim needing confirmation, whereas A, C and D answer an unrelated AI-audience activation problem without defining the requested events or establishing the necessary profile entitlements.

A and D propose a plausible BI-extension connection and Workspace comparisons with entitlement disclosure but little metric governance or sales reconciliation, B adds executive briefs and measure guides without resolving that reconciliation gap, and C best addresses Power BI retention, metric ownership, data movement, effort and tolerances while still failing to specify the Salesforce reconciliation procedure or substantiate the asserted cause of existing differences.

A gives concrete automated and manual checks, document sampling and retest evidence but leaves the verifying reviewer as a placeholder and broader document remediation optional, D offers a useful WCAG audit and template-testing approach without document remediation or accountable verification, C provides generic component delivery and testing without accessibility criteria, and B merely requests discovery inputs.

A covers routine work for all four products but omits incident accountability, integration operations and fee boundaries, B provides useful DAM routines and effort while neglecting most of the service scope, C offers similarly narrow Sites monitoring and releases, and D supplies twelve-month ownership, integration checks, reporting, allocations and separate-estimate boundaries but retains an unfilled service-level schedule and incomplete monitoring and escalation detail.

notes: All seven presented requirements and their A-D answer blocks were judged; unpresented requirements were not scored, and no displayed answer required a word-limit deduction.
Client facts and Adobe terminology earned credit only when connected to a relevant delivery method, dependency, acceptance check or accountable output.

Several answers substitute template creation, lead scoring or audience activation for the specific migration, routing or measurement requirement, leaving important operational failure cases unanswered.

The more complete answers still leave gaps in test evidence, reconciliation mechanics, repeated-enquiry handling, named verification or contractual service commitments, so none merits an exceptional score.
Product-specific sync, profile-entitlement and governance-enforcement details were treated as requiring confirmation where uncertain, rather than asserted to be product errors.
